attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, written in his voice. This is not the passage where he quotes what he told Barrett.

semantics.note: The normalised claim keeps the shared-cause wording ('emanate from the same dynamics') and the 'pure LLMs' qualifier. It is an unhedged causal explanation, so it is scorable in principle.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'pure LLMs' and of 'stable, revisable world models' is ordinary and fair. The support and contradiction conditions are demanding, but that suits a mechanistic causal claim. The result does not depend on how the terms are read, because no evidence meets either condition.

evidence.note: FreshQA (2023) puts current-news failures down to missing up-to-date knowledge, not to a missing world model. It does not test the proposed mechanism, and it covers a different period and different models.
Shows incoherent implicit world models in bounded synthetic domains. That fits Marcus's general concern, but it does not test breaking-news errors or hallucinations, or a shared cause.

Othello study: a synthetic game model forms internal board representations that interventions can manipulate. This undercuts a 'only correlations' view in a toy setting, but says nothing about real-world news or hallucination errors.

PNAS 2026 (available before the cutoff) shows a statistical, calibration-based handle on hallucination. It does not measure world models or breaking news, so it neither rejects nor confirms the shared mechanism.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no controlled study that ties world-representation deficits to both breaking-news errors and hallucinations, and none that rejects that link. e1 points to missing information, e3 shows emergent representations in a toy setting, and e4 gives a statistical account of hallucination. All four are context only, so the causal claim is checked but not settled by the cutoff.
